title: Defect-mediated orientational ordering in stripe-forming magnetic systems
authors: Premarun Barik, Johan van Lierop, Robert L. Stamps
abstract: We investigate the nonequilibrium development of orientational order in a two-dimensional stripe-forming magnetic system with competing interactions. Following a quench into the stripe-ordered regime, horizontal and vertical stripes organize into orientational regions(super-domains) separated by characteristic defects. We show that the evolution towards a globally oriented stripe state is mediated by the motion and elimination of these defects, with T-junctions providing a direct microscopic measure of super-domain reorganization. The T-junction population reveals distinct dynamical regimes associated with super-domain formation, growth, and equilibration. Temperature, system size, and equilibrium stripe width modify the characteristic time scales of this evolution, while thermal fluctuations produce a finite defect population at higher temperatures. We further show that the defect dynamics observed in real space are reflected in the structure factor, providing a reciprocal-space signature of defect elimination. These results establish a microscopic defect-based description of orientational ordering in stripe-forming magnetic systems.
summary: This work develops a microscopic theory for how stripe-forming magnetic systems achieve global orientational order after a sudden quench. It demonstrates that this ordering process is governed by the dynamics of topological defects, particularly T-junctions, which move and eliminate over time. The key finding is the quantitative link between tracking these defects in real space and observing corresponding changes in the system's structure factor in reciprocal space.
main_problem: The paper investigates the non-equilibrium process by which a two-dimensional stripe-forming magnetic system develops global orientational order following a quench.
main_result: Global order is shown to be mediated by the motion and elimination of topological defects, specifically T-junctions, which provides a microscopic, defect-based description of the ordering process.
method: The study uses Monte Carlo simulations to track the real-space evolution of spin configurations and compares these defect dynamics to signatures observed in the structure factor in reciprocal space.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D stripe-forming magnetic model described by an Ising Hamiltonian incorporating nearest-neighbor exchange and long-range dipolar interactions. The evolution is studied by quenching the system into the stripe-ordered regime.
key_observables: T-junctions, corners, I-junctions (defects), the T-junction population dynamics, and the structure factor in reciprocal space.
important_parameters: Temperature (T), relative strength of interactions (delta), and system size. The dynamics are characterized by distinct regimes (formation, growth, equilibration).
main_assumptions: The dipolar interaction is approximated using a finite cut-off radius (Rc), and the analysis relies on comparing real-space defect elimination rates with reciprocal-space structure factor changes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate stripe pattern evolution after a quench, showing defect formation and subsequent elimination leading to global order. Another figure compares defect elimination rates measured in real space versus reciprocal space.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, details the simulation methodology (quenching, defect tracking), analyzes the time evolution through distinct dynamical regimes based on defect counts, and finally confirms the microscopic mechanism by showing the correspondence between real-space defect decay and reciprocal-space structure factor sharpening.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between the dynamics of topological defects (T-junctions) in real space and the measurable signatures in the structure factor (reciprocal space) provides a powerful, generalizable diagnostic tool for studying non-equilibrium ordering in complex many-body systems.

Local horizontal and vertical stripe regions grow with time, eventually producing a globally ordered stripe state. Snapshots are shown at t=10, 122, 1232, 4937, 12459, and 100000 Monte Carlo steps.

FIG. 4. A schematic illustration of T-junction motion lead- ing to the shrinkage of a vertical diamond-shaped super- domain. The small boxes indicate regions where spin flips are most probable, resulting in successive displacement of the T-junctions and reduction of the super-domain area. Black lines are included as guides to the eye to identify the super- domain boundary.

FIG. 3. Schematic illustration of the different defect types associated with orientational super-domains. (a) Horizontal super-domain embedded in a vertical-stripe background. The boundary contains left and right T-junctions together with up and down I-junctions. (b) Vertical super-domain embedded in a horizontal-stripe background. In this case, the boundary contains up and down T-junctions together with left and right I-junctions. Representative corners along the super-domain boundary are also indicated.

FIG. 6. Evolution of the T-junction count with Monte Carlo steps for L = 100 and δ = 1.1 at (a) T = 0.1 and (b) T = 0.3. The shaded regions, labelled I–IV, indicate four successive stages of the evolution. In regime I, the T-junction population increases as locally formed horizontal and vertical stripes or- ganize into orientational super-domains. In regime II, the T- junction count decreases as the super-domains reorganize and grow through the motion and elimination of their boundary defects.
